title.en: Sound: hands-on activities from the textbook

text.en: Sound is a vibration you can feel. Chapter 10's activities let you pluck, tap and spin to see how it travels.

Activity 10.1 stretches a rubber band across an open box and plucks it. You hear a sound while it vibrates.
Activity 10.2 strikes a tuning fork on a rubber pad. You hear the sound in any direction, so it travels in all directions from the source.
Activity 10.3 compares hearing a knock on a desk through air and through the desk with your ear against it. Sound also travels through solids.
Activity 10.4 taps two spoons under water and still hears the sound, so liquids carry sound too.
Activity 10.5 uses a slinky with a mark on one turn. A push makes compressions and rarefactions travel along while the marked turn only moves back and forth, so sound is a longitudinal wave.
Activity 10.6 stretches a cellophane sheet over a container and sounds a metal plate near it. Grains on the sheet jump because the sheet vibrates.
Activities 10.7 and 10.8 use a sound app. Raising the frequency makes the pitch higher, and a thin rubber band vibrates faster than a thick one.
So frequency decides pitch, and a higher frequency means a shorter time period.

problem.en: Why does a thin rubber band give a higher pitch than a thick one?

text.en: Higher frequency means a higher pitch.

prompt.en: What do the slinky and the cellophane activities show about sound?

requiredIdeas.en: Sound is a longitudinal wave of compressions
The medium vibrates but does not travel

commonMisconceptions.en: Thinking sound travels in a vacuum

points.en: It travels through solids, liquids and gases.
Sound is a longitudinal wave of compressions and rarefactions.
Higher frequency gives higher pitch and a shorter time period.
